'''Claire M. Fraser''' (born November 5, 1955) is an American [[genome]] scientist and [[microbiologist]] who has worked in microbial genomics and genome medicine.<ref name=started>{{cite web |url=https://www.aaas.org/membership/member-spotlight/claire-m-fraser-pioneer-whos-just-getting-started |title="Claire M. Fraser Is a Pioneer Who's Just Getting Started" |author=Katherine Lee |date=December 17, 2018 |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref> Her research has contributed to the understanding of the diversity and evolution of microbial life. Fraser is the director of the Institute for Genome Sciences at the [[University of Maryland School of Medicine]] in [[Baltimore, MD]], where she holds the Dean's Endowed Professorship in the School of Medicine.  She has joint faculty appointments at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in the Departments of Medicine and Microbiology/Immunology. In 2019, she began serving a one-year term as President-Elect for the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS), which will be followed by a one-year term as AAAS president starting in February 2020 and a one-year term as chair of the Board of Directors in February 2021.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/microbial-genomics-trailblazer-claire-m-fraser-named-aaas-president-elect |title=Microbial Genomics Trailblazer Claire M. Fraser Named AAAS President-Elect}}</ref>

==Early life==
Claire M. Fraser was born on November 5, 1955, in Boston, Massachusetts.<ref>{{Cite web |title="Claire M. Fraser." Maryland State Archives, MSA SC 3520-1524 |url=https://msa.maryland.gov/megafile/msa/speccol/sc3500/sc3520/015200/015241/html/15241bio.html#:~:text=a%20lifetime%E2%80%9D1-,Claire%20M.,1955,%20in%20Boston,%20Massachusetts. |access-date=March 24, 2026 |website=msa.maryland.gov}}</ref> Fraser was raised by a high school principal and an elementary school teacher in [[Saugus, MA]] a suburb of [[Boston, MA]].<ref name=started/> She performed well at school and was always interested in learning.<ref name=started/> She became interested in science after being taught biology in high school.<ref name=started/> At [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] (RPI), during her senior year, she performed independent research in a research lab.<ref name=started/>

==Education==
Fraser received her [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in Biology from [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] in 1977 and her [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] degree in Pharmacology at the [[State University of New York at Buffalo]] in 1981 with a thesis entitled "Autoantibodies and monoclonal antibodies to beta-adrenergic receptors : their role in receptor characterization and human physiology".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://library.buffalo.edu/archives/ubpeople/detail.html?ID=5198 |title=Claire Fraser-Liggett}}{{dead link|date=October 2026}}</ref>

==Career==
Fraser has authored more than 300 publications with more than 50,000 citations, edited four books, and served on the editorial boards of nine scientific journals.<ref name=google-scholar>{{cite web |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=0%2C44&q=claire+fraser&oq= |title=Google Scholar}}</ref> She is included on 23 issued patents and 19 published patents<ref name=google-scholar/>

===Genomics===

Fraser's work on the 2001 [[Amerithrax]] investigation led to the identification of four genetic mutations in the [[anthrax]] spores that enabled the FBI to trace the material back to its original source.<ref name="Bacillus anthracis comparative geno"/> This effort catalyzed the development of the field of microbial forensics. She is an expert in microbial forensics and the growing concern about dual uses – research that can provide knowledge and technologies that could be misapplied.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Fraser|first1=Claire M.|last2=Dando|first2=Malcolm R.|title=Genomics and future biological weapons: the need for preventive action by the biomedical community|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=29|issue=3|year=2001|pages=253–256|issn=1061-4036|doi=10.1038/ng763|pmid=11687792|s2cid=11211547}}</ref>

Fraser has led NIAID-funded efforts in the genomics of infectious disease, including the current iteration of the Genome Centers for Infectious Disease.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/genomic-centers-infectious-diseases |title=Genomic Centers for Infectious Diseases (GCID) |access-date=March 30, 2019}}</ref> Past and current studies funded through these initiatives aim to explore the dynamic interactions between high-priority pathogens, hosts, their microbiota, the immune system, and the environment, with the goal to provide a comprehensive understanding of the determinants of infectious disease with hypothesis-driven research using high-throughput "-omics" technologies.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gcid.igs.umaryland.edu/ |title=Overview, Host, Pathogen and the Microbiome: Determinants of Disease Outcome |access-date=March 30, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Richter|first1=Taylor K. Fraser's current research is part of the [[Human Microbiome Project]] and is focused on how the structure and function of microbial communities in the human gastrointestinal tract change in association with diseases such as [[obesity]] and [[inflammatory bowel disease]], and how these communities respond to interventions including oral [[vaccination]] and [[probiotics]] administration.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Yan|last2=Brady|first2=Arthur|last3=Jones|first3=Cheron|last4=Song|first4=Yang|last5=Darton|first5=Thomas C.|last6=Jones|first6=Claire|last7=Blohmke|first7=Christoph J.|last8=Pollard|first8=Andrew J.|last9=Magder|first9=Laurence S.|last10=Fasano|first10=Alessio|last11=Sztein|first11=Marcelo B.|last12=Fraser|first12=Claire M.|last13=Dominguez Bello|first13=Maria Gloria|title=Compositional and Functional Differences in the Human Gut Microbiome Correlate with Clinical Outcome following Infection with Wild-Type Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi |journal=mBio|volume=9|issue=3|year=2018|issn=2150-7511|doi=10.1128/mBio.00686-18|pmid=29739901|pmc=5941076|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Eloe-Fadrosh|first1=Emiley A.|last2=Brady|first2=Arthur|last3=Crabtree|first3=Jonathan|last4=Drabek|first4=Elliott F.|last5=Ma|first5=Bing|last6=Mahurkar|first6=Anup|last7=Ravel|first7=Jacques|last8=Haverkamp|first8=Miriam|last9=Fiorino|first9=Anne-Maria|last10=Botelho|first10=Christine|last11=Andreyeva|first11=Irina|last12=Hibberd|first12=Patricia L.|last13=Fraser|first13=Claire M.|last14=McFall-Ngai|first14=Margaret J.|title=Functional Dynamics of the Gut Microbiome in Elderly People during Probiotic Consumption|journal=mBio|volume=6|issue=2|year=2015|issn=2150-7511|doi=10.1128/mBio.00231-15|pmid=25873374|pmc=4453556|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Advisory panels and editorial boards===
In 2019, Fraser is serving a one-year term as President-Elect for the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS), which will be followed by a one-year term as AAAS president starting in February 2020 and a one-year term as chair of the Board of Directors in February 2021.<ref name=AAAS/> In accepting the nomination to be a candidate for AAAS President, Fraser expressed a desire to use this position to be an ardent spokesperson for science and to promote application of the scientific method to the solution of our most pressing problems, including [[climate change]], [[antimicrobial resistance]] as well as [[food security]], [[water security]], and [[energy security]].<ref name=quote>{{cite web |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2019-01/uoms-ucf010819.ph |title=UMSOM's Claire Fraser appointed president-elect of AAAS |author=University of Maryland School of Medicine |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref> She notes that "our ability to respond to these challenges has been hampered to a considerable extent by a lack of adequate funding, a tendency to fund 'safer' research projects, and a relative lack of public trust in science.".<ref name=quote/>

Fraser has been an editor for journals ''[[mBio]]'', ''[[Journal of Bacteriology]]'', ''[[Microbial Genomics (journal)]]'', ''Molecular Case Studies'', and ''[[DNA and Cell Biology]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mbio.asm.org/content/board-editors |title=mBio Board of Editors |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://journals.asm.org/content/jb/187/2/local/masthead.pdf |title=Journal of Bacteriology Masthead |date=January 2005 |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://mgen.microbiologyresearch.org/content/journal/mgen/editorial |title="Microbial Genomics Editorial Board" |publisher=Microbiology Society |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://molecularcasestudies.cshlp.org/site/misc/about.xhtml |title=About Cold Spring Harbor Molecular Case Studies |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://home.liebertpub.com/publications/dna-and-cell-biology/13/editorial-board |title=DNA and Cell Biology About This Journal |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref> Since 2006, Fraser has also served as a member of the Board of Directors of Becton, Dickinson and Company (BD), a Fortune 500 medical technology company.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://investors.bd.com/phoenix.zhtml?c=64106&p=irol-newsArticle_pf&ID=909346 |title=BD Board of Directors Elects Dr. Claire M. Fraser-Liggett |access-date=March 30, 2019}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Fraser was previously married to [[Craig Venter]]. Since 2013, she has been married to Jack Kammer, an author who examines gender issues from a male point of view.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.com/Jack-Kammer/e/B001KDBG9A?ref=sr_ntt_srch_lnk_2&qid=1554047791&sr=1-2-catcorr |title="Amazon Jack Kammer" |website=Amazon |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref> Fraser has owned several standard poodles, including Shadow whose genome was sequenced.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.genomeweb.com/archive/venter-fraser-use-pet-poodle-celeratigr-dog-genome-project#.XKDhr_ZFw_Y |title="Venter, Fraser Use Pet Poodle for Celera/TIGR Dog Genome Project" |date=May 10, 2002 |access-date=March 31, 2019}}</ref>
